Technical deep dive · Triple Roman Domination

Model, algorithms, and experiments.

Formal definition, ILP formulation correction, GA and ACO metaheuristics, and results on 362 graphs.

See the correction of the exact model See the algorithms See the results
  • Integer Linear Programming

Definition

The problem, formally.

In a graph G, h assigns each vertex a label in {0, 1, 2, 3, 4}; AN(v) is the active neighbourhood of v.

Triple Roman Domination function

Σu ∈ N[v] h(u) ≥ 3 + |AN(v)|, ∀ v ∈ V(G)

The weight of h is the sum of labels; γ3R(G) is the smallest valid weight. The decision version is NP-complete.

The overview uses the same inequality: every active neighbour contributes h(u) − 1, and the vertex itself contributes h(v).

Reduction: an optimal function exists without label 1; the work therefore uses only {0, 2, 3, 4}.

The bounds used as reference in the work: γ3R(G) ≥ ⌈4n / (Δ+1)⌉ for connected graphs with Δ ≥ 3 and n ≥ 2 (Valenzuela-Tripodoro et al., 2024), and γ3R(G) ≤ 3n/2 for connected graphs with δ ≥ 2 (Hajjari et al., 2023).

Exact model

A published formulation that accepts an invalid solution.

Inspect the correction and counterexample

The only Integer Linear Programming formulation available for the problem (Vengaldas et al., 2023) uses six binary variables per vertex and four families of constraints. The constraint responsible for zero-labelled vertices is linearly too loose: there are labellings that satisfy it without being triple Roman domination functions.

The faulty constraint

pv + qv + rv + sv + Σu∈N(v) su + ⅓ Σu∈N(v) qu + ½ (tv + xv) ≥ 1

Here q, r, and s indicate labels 2, 3, and 4; t and x indicate the existence of some neighbour labelled 2 and some neighbour labelled 3. Summing fractions lets two neighbours labelled 2 “pay” the constraint together with the indicator t, even though two neighbours labelled 2 are not enough under the definition.

The authors refine that model into two further versions and show they are equivalent to one another. Since the faulty constraint is precisely the one modelling zero-labelled vertices and it remains in all three versions, all three inherit the flaw.

The proposed formulation

min Σv∈V (2qv + 3rv + 4sv) (2qv + 3rv + 4sv) + Σu∈N(v) (qu + 2ru + 3su) ≥ 3 qv + rv + sv ≤ 1, qv, rv, sv ∈ {0,1}

The constraint is the definition itself written in binary variables, after cancelling the |AN(v)| term: a neighbour labelled 2 contributes 1, one labelled 3 contributes 2, and one labelled 4 contributes 3 — exactly “sends everything but one legion”. Dropping the label 1 through the theorem above reduces the model from 6|V| variables and 4|V| constraints to 3|V| variables and 2|V| constraints.

Algorithms

Two metaheuristics, the same solution format.

Both algorithms search vectors in {0, 2, 3, 4}n and minimize their sum; only the exploration differs.

FLGA

Genetic algorithm.

Inspect operators and ablations
  • Initial population by heuristic: four variants were compared. H1 draws a vertex, labels it 2, and zeroes its neighbourhood; H2 does the same with label 4 and then tries to lower labels; H3 walks the vertices in decreasing order of degree; H4 mixes the three in equal parts. H4 won and defines the FLGA.
  • Repair instead of discard: crossover and mutation produce infeasible solutions often. Rather than rejecting them, the feasibilityCheck routine walks the violated vertices and raises the label to the minimum that restores feasibility. The population is fully feasible at the end of every generation.
  • Greedy reduction: decreaseLabels tries to lower each label (4 → 3 → 2 → 0) and undoes any change that breaks feasibility for the vertex or its active neighbourhood. This is what keeps the repair step from accumulating needless slack.
  • Operators: tournament selection, one- or two-point crossover drawn for each pair, mutation replacing one position with a random label, and elitism preserving ⌈population × rate⌉ individuals.
  • Stopping: a maximum number of generations, or a maximum number of consecutive generations without improvement — whichever comes first.

ACO-FL

Ant colony optimization with local search.

Inspect construction, pheromones, and local search

The implementation follows the Max-Min Ant System inside the Hyper-Cube Framework: every vertex carries a pheromone τv ∈ [0,1], initialized at 0.5 and bounded to [0.001, 0.999].

  • Construction: each ant picks vertices to receive label 4 and zeroes their neighbourhood, until the auxiliary graph is exhausted. The choice uses deg(u) · τu: with a fixed probability it takes the maximum, otherwise it draws by proportional roulette.
  • Extend and reduce: extendSolution promotes a fraction of the vertices to label 4, deliberately making the solution more expensive in order to escape local minima; reduceSolution then walks the vertices in decreasing order of degree, lowering labels while feasibility holds.
  • RVNS local search: it destroys part of the solution, rebuilds, extends, and reduces. The intensity of the destruction grows with the neighbourhood level k, which rises on every iteration without improvement and returns to 1 as soon as a better solution appears.
  • Pheromones guided by convergence: the factor φ decides the weight of the iteration best against the global best — only the iteration best while φ < 0.4, only the global best once φ ≥ 0.8. If φ goes past 0.99, pheromones are reinitialized to avoid stagnation.

Protocol

How the experiments were set up.

Inspect environment and parameters
  • Instances — 362 graphs: 50 sparse matrices from the BAI collection, 186 from Harwell-Boeing, 56 graphs from Miscellaneous Networks, 10 graphs from each classic family (cycles, paths, stars, and trees), and 30 Erdős-Rényi random graphs from 25 to 250 vertices with connection probability 0.2, 0.5, and 0.8.
  • Exact reference: the ILP model was implemented in Python with Pyomo and NetworkX. The free CPLEX edition is limited to a thousand variables and a thousand constraints, which covers graphs of up to 333 vertices; beyond that, CBC was used. Each instance had at most 900 seconds, and the solver returns the best solution found — which is not always provably optimal.
  • Parameter tuning: irace was used on 115 graphs selected from the study set. The described protocol does not establish an independent test outside tuning graphs; results describe performance on this set, without a generalization guarantee.
  • Environment: Intel Core i5-8265U at 1.60 GHz, 8 GB of RAM, Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS. Metaheuristics in C++ compiled with G++ 11.4.0 and the flags -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Ofast -finline-functions -march=native.

Results

ACO-FL and FLGA, compared with the exact reference when available.

Gap compares the best metaheuristic result with the ILP reference. ACO-FL led most observed cases, but FLGA wins on some graphs.

Results and impact communicated

The three metrics behind every claim.

Runtime, fitness, and gap were defined before the experiments and applied to both algorithms and the exact model.

Criterion 1

Runtime

Seconds per instance in the same environment. Lower is better if quality and search budgets are comparable; speed alone does not decide the winner.

Criterion 2

Fitness, the weight of the solution

Sum of labels of a feasible solution. Lower is better; an infeasible solution is excluded from quality comparisons.

Criterion 3

Relative gap

Percentage difference against the ILP reference. Zero means matching that reference; it means matching the optimum only if certified.

How it is computed

gap = (best − ILP) / ILP

The numerator uses the better of the two metaheuristics.

Research contributions:

  • Corrected formulation: a counterexample demonstrating the published ILP flaw.
  • Implementation: genetic-algorithm and ant-colony metaheuristics.
  • Reusable dataset: graphs, outputs, and ILP references preserved. Only proven optimal values should be treated as optima; others are time-limited reference solutions.
  • Experimental selection: RVNS local search and H4 initial population compared under the same protocol.
  • Observed distribution: 6 of 362 graphs exceeded 50% of the reference. This describes the result tail; it does not imply others reached the optimum or that 50% loss is acceptable.

Limits of what was measured

What the numbers do not say.

  • Reference without proof of optimality: under a 900 s limit, an unstarred ILP value is a feasible solution (upper bound), not the optimum. Gap against this reference is not an upper bound on optimality error; when the heuristic costs more than the reference, it may underestimate the true distance. If it costs less, the gap may be negative. Use the solver bound for a certified-distance estimate.
  • Relative gap and absolute cost: on g200-.8, 12 versus optimum 8 means 4 more units and a 50% gap. Neither measure is wrong: together they show absolute and relative loss. With a small optimum, each unit contributes more to the percentage.
  • One run per instance. The metaheuristics are stochastic, and the reported results do not come from multiple runs with confidence intervals, which rules out claiming small differences between the two algorithms.
  • Open work. Widening the hyperparameter search, testing other selection, crossover, mutation, and elitism strategies for the GA, evaluating other choice mechanisms for the ACO, and cutting runtime through implementation optimizations.
